Gift, key and property incident entries in the client record
Incident reports under SAF-02
Telephone report notes and the written or internet abuse report, with dates and times, kept in the confidential report file
Annual review of exploitation incidents

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] staff, affiliated home care aides and volunteers, in dealings with all clients, applicants and their representatives, whether payer-funded or private-pay
policies.purpose: To ensure every client and applicant is treated without discrimination, receives reasonable accommodation for disability, and can understand the services, rights and agreements offered by [AGENCY NAME].
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate against any client or applicant because of race, color, national origin, disability, age, religion or sex. This applies to intake, service planning, staffing, scheduling, discharge and all other dealings. It applies equally to clients paid for by a managed care plan or other payer and to private-pay clients. [AGENCY NAME] complies with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. 2000d) and the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 U.S.C. 12101 et seq.). The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act (HSC §1796.10 et seq.) sets no specific language-access rule, so the interpreter and translation commitments below are an operator standard adopted by [AGENCY NAME]. We provide reasonable accommodations for disabilities. We offer a qualified interpreter or translated documents, free of charge, to clients with limited English proficiency. Eligibility decisions are based only on whether the client's needs fit non-medical home care, whether we serve the area and whether we have staff available (see SVC-01). They are never based on a protected characteristic.

definitions.definition: Treating a person less favorably, denying or limiting services, or applying different terms because of race, color, national origin, disability, age, religion or sex.
A client or representative who does not speak English as a primary language and has a limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English.

A modification of a policy, procedure, communication method or service delivery that lets a person with a disability use and benefit from the agency's services, unless it would fundamentally change the service or create an undue burden.

A person able to interpret accurately and impartially between English and the client's language. Staff aides are used only if they are qualified and the client agrees. Family members or minors are not used unless the client specifically requests it and understands that free interpretation is available.

procedures: The Administrator or designee ensures that the nondiscrimination statement is printed in the client packet, on the agency's website and in the service agreement. The statement says [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, disability, age, religion or sex.
At intake the Client Care Supervisor asks every applicant what language they prefer for speaking and for written material. The answer is recorded in the client record.

The Client Care Supervisor asks whether the client or representative needs any accommodation, such as large print, reading aloud, hearing or speech aids, extra time, or a home visit instead of an office visit. The accommodation is recorded and added to the service plan (SVC-02).

When a client or representative has limited English proficiency, staff offer a qualified interpreter or translated documents at no charge. This applies at intake, assessment, service agreement review, rights notices, complaint handling and discharge.

The Administrator or designee keeps a list of qualified interpreter resources, including telephone or video interpreter services, and bilingual staff who are qualified. The list is updated at least annually and is available to the Client Care Supervisor and Scheduler.

The Client Care Supervisor provides the client rights notice (CR-01), the grievance procedure (CR-02) and the service agreement (CR-06) in the client's language where translated versions exist. Where no translation exists, the supervisor uses an interpreter to read the documents and notes the date, method and interpreter in the record.

Staff do not require clients to bring their own interpreter, do not charge for interpretation, and do not use language ability as a reason to deny or delay services. Eligibility is decided under SVC-01.

When possible, the Scheduler matches clients with aides who speak the client's language. Language match is a preference for care quality, not a basis for refusing to serve a client when no matching aide is available. In that case an interpreter is arranged for supervisory visits and complaint handling.

Aides and staff do not make comments or take actions based on a client's or co-worker's protected characteristics. A client may not be refused service because of such characteristics. If a client asks to change aides because of a protected characteristic of the aide, the Administrator or designee consults the licensee and responds with a decision based on this policy and applicable law. The request is not simply granted.

Reasonable accommodation requests are decided promptly by the Client Care Supervisor and Administrator. If an accommodation is not provided, the Administrator documents the reason and offers an alternative. The client is told of the right to file a grievance.
Staff who see or hear discrimination report it to the Administrator or designee the same day. The Administrator documents the report, investigates under CR-02 and PER-09, and informs the licensee.
Clients may complain about discrimination under CR-02 without fear of retaliation. The Administrator or designee gives a written response as set out in CR-02.

All staff receive training on this policy at hire and annually. The training covers nondiscrimination, accommodation of disabilities and use of interpreters. Completion is recorded in the training log (TRN-05).
At least annually, the Administrator reviews grievances and incidents involving discrimination or language access and reports results to the licensee under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Treats all clients with respect and without discrimination, uses interpreter resources through the supervisor and reports discrimination.
Records language preference and accommodation needs, arranges interpreters and translated documents, and applies nondiscriminatory eligibility decisions.
Matches language where possible without denying service, and uses interpreters on scheduling calls when needed.
Maintains the interpreter list, decides accommodation disputes, investigates complaints and keeps training current.
Ensures resources for interpretation and accommodations and receives annual reports.

documentation: Nondiscrimination statement in client packet and service agreement
Client record entry for language preference and accommodations
Interpreter or translation log (date, method, interpreter used)
Accommodation requests and decisions
Discrimination reports and complaint files under CR-02
Annual training records (TRN-05)
Annual review of grievances and language access

policies.title: Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: The Client Care Supervisor, Scheduler/Registry and Billing Coordinator, Administrator and designee, and all staff who discuss services, rates or billing with clients and applicants
policies.purpose: To make sure every client or representative receives a clear written agreement before services start. The agreement states what will be provided, at what price and on what terms, and how to ask questions or dispute a bill.
policies.policy: The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act (HSC §1796.10 et seq.) sets no specific contract terms. The requirements in this policy are an operator standard adopted by [AGENCY NAME]. No services begin until the client or the client's legally authorized representative has received a copy of a written service agreement and signed it. The agreement states the services to be provided, the schedule, the rates, the minimum visit length and the cancellation terms. It states the scope limits and that the services are non-medical. It explains how billing works and how to dispute a bill. The client receives a copy before services start. Rates and terms for payer-funded clients follow the applicable payer contract and are also explained to the client in writing.

definitions.definition: The written agreement between [AGENCY NAME] and the client or representative describing the services, schedule, rates, minimum visit, cancellation terms, scope limits and billing terms.
The shortest period of time for which a visit is scheduled and billed, as stated in the agreement.
A person legally authorized to sign for the client, such as a conservator or agent under a power of attorney. Proof is kept in the record.

Services limited to home care services described in HSC §1796.12(n). These do not include skilled nursing or medical care, or medication assistance that would require administration or oversight by a licensed health care professional.

procedures: After the assessment and acceptance decision under SVC-01, the Client Care Supervisor prepares the service agreement using the agency's approved template. The template is reviewed under GOV-04.
The agreement states the services to be provided, drawn from the draft service plan (SVC-02), and the days and hours of service.

The agreement states each hourly rate, any different rates for nights, weekends or holidays, the minimum visit length, how mileage or transportation is charged, if applicable, and any other fee. If there are no other fees, it says so.

The agreement states cancellation terms, including how much notice the client must give, any fee for late cancellation, and how [AGENCY NAME] notifies the client if it must cancel or if an aide is late or unavailable (SVC-05).

The agreement states that [AGENCY NAME] provides non-medical home care only. It lists the main things aides may not do, including skilled nursing tasks and medication administration (see PRG-03 and SVC-04), and says the agency will refer the client to a licensed provider for those needs.

The agreement explains billing: when invoices are issued, the payment due date, accepted forms of payment, and what happens if a payment is late. It names the agency contact for billing questions, with [PHONE] and [ADDRESS].

The agreement explains how to dispute a bill. The client may contact the Scheduler/Registry and Billing Coordinator by phone or in writing. The Coordinator reviews the visit records and timekeeping, and responds in writing within 10 business days. A client who is not satisfied may use the grievance procedure in CR-02.

The agreement includes the client rights notice (CR-01), the grievance procedure (CR-02), the privacy notice (CR-03), the gift and money notice (CR-04), and the nondiscrimination and language statement (CR-05).
The agreement lists the conditions under which [AGENCY NAME] may end services and how much notice it gives, consistent with SVC-08. It also states that the client may end services at any time.

The agreement identifies the payer. For clients funded by a managed care plan or other payer, it explains what the payer covers, what the client may owe, and that the plan or payer terms govern authorized hours (SVC-09).

The Client Care Supervisor reviews the agreement with the client or representative in plain language before signing. Where the client has limited English proficiency or a disability that affects reading, the supervisor uses an interpreter, translated documents or other accommodation under CR-05.

The client or authorized representative signs and dates the agreement. An agency representative also signs. The client may take time to consider the agreement and is not pressured to sign on the spot.
The Client Care Supervisor gives the client a complete copy before the first visit and notes the date and method of delivery in the record. Services do not start until this is done.
The original agreement goes into the client record (REC-01). The Scheduler/Registry and Billing Coordinator enters the rates and terms into the billing system exactly as in the agreement.

If rates or terms change, the Client Care Supervisor or Coordinator gives the client written notice of at least 30 days before the change, and the client signs an amended agreement. The client may decline and end services.
The Coordinator reviews invoices for accuracy against visit records (SVC-06) before they are sent. Billing errors are corrected and credited promptly. Billing practices follow GOV-06.

responsibilities.duty: Prepares and reviews the agreement with the client, obtains signatures, and gives the client a copy before services begin.
Enters rates correctly, issues accurate invoices, handles billing disputes and corrects errors.
Approves the agreement template and rates, reviews disputed bills, and ensures no services start without a signed agreement.
Sets rates and fee policies and ensures that billing is honest and consistent with the agreements.

documentation: Signed service agreement and proof of delivery of a copy
Authorized representative documentation, if applicable
Rate and fee schedule in effect at the time of signing
Written notices of rate or term changes and amended agreements
Billing dispute log and written responses
Invoices and supporting visit records

policies.title: Client Intake, Eligibility and Assessment
policies.applies_to: The Client Care Supervisor, Scheduler/Registry and Billing Coordinator, Administrator and designee, and any staff who take inquiries or conduct assessments
policies.purpose: To accept only clients whose needs can be safely met by non-medical home care services, to assess each client's needs and home, and to refer people who need skilled care to the right provider.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a Home Care Organization that arranges non-medical home care services by affiliated home care aides, as described in HSC §1796.12(j) and (n). We accept only clients whose needs fit those services. Clients who need skilled care are referred to a licensed home health agency or other appropriate provider. The program description submitted under HCS 281 Section B5 states the services, area, hours and population we serve, and intake decisions follow it. Before accepting a client, we check the service area and whether we have staff available. The assessment covers the client's needs, home safety, medication-assistance needs and emergency contacts. The Act sets no assessment form or timeline, so the steps and time frames below are an operator standard.

definitions.definition: Non-medical services for a client who cannot perform them because of age or disability, such as bathing, dressing, feeding, exercising, hygiene and grooming, transferring, ambulating, positioning, toileting and incontinence care, assisting with self-administered medication, housekeeping, meals, laundry, transportation, correspondence, phone calls, shopping and companionship (HSC §1796.12(n)).
Care requiring a licensed health care professional, such as nursing assessments, wound care, injections, medication administration or oversight, and other medical treatment.

Medication the client takes themselves. The aide may assist with reminders, opening containers or handing items to the client, but may not administer it or assist with medication that would otherwise require administration or oversight by a licensed health care professional.
The process of receiving an inquiry, screening for fit, completing the assessment, deciding on acceptance and starting a service plan.

procedures: The staff member who takes an inquiry completes the Intake Screening Form. It records the caller's name, relationship to the client, the client's address and phone, the care needs requested, the payer, urgency, and preferred language (CR-05).

During the screening the staff member checks that the client's address is in the service area listed in the program description (PRG-06) and checks with the Scheduler whether staff are available for the requested days and hours. If not, the client is told on the same call and referred to other providers.

The staff member explains that [AGENCY NAME] provides non-medical home care only. If the caller describes needs for skilled care, such as injections, wound care, catheter care, oxygen management, or medication administration, the Client Care Supervisor reviews the case and refers the client to a licensed home health agency or other appropriate provider. We do not accept a client when the need for skilled care is the primary need.

If a client needs both skilled care and non-medical services, we may accept the non-medical part only if the client's licensed provider is coordinating the skilled care and the Client Care Supervisor documents it. We never perform the skilled tasks.

The Client Care Supervisor schedules the in-home assessment, with the client and, when the client agrees, a family member or representative. The Client Care Supervisor performs the assessment within [3] business days of the screening, or sooner if the need is urgent.

The assessment documents: the client's diagnoses and functional abilities as reported, mobility and transfer needs, bathing, toileting, eating and cognition needs, behaviors that affect care, equipment in use, allergies, and language and communication needs.

The assessment documents medication-assistance needs. This means which medications the client takes, who sets them up, and whether the client can take them without administration or oversight by a licensed professional. If the client cannot, the Client Care Supervisor asks the client or family to arrange licensed support, and the aide's role is limited as set out in SVC-04.

The supervisor completes a home safety check that covers trip hazards, lighting, stairs, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, pets, firearms or other hazards, working utilities, and any risk to the aide (SAF-05). Hazards are discussed with the client and recorded with the plan to resolve them.

The assessment records the client's emergency contacts, physician, preferred hospital, any advance directives the client chooses to share, and a plan for emergencies (SAF-04 and SVC-07). The supervisor does not decide medical matters and does not hold the client's medical records beyond what the client gives.

The supervisor reviews the assessment against the program description and decides whether to accept. The decision is based on whether the needs fit non-medical home care, whether the home is safe, whether we serve the area, and whether staffing is available. It is never based on a protected characteristic (CR-05). The decision is documented, and the Administrator or designee reviews any denial or conditional acceptance.

If the client is declined, the supervisor tells the client or representative the reason and gives referrals to other resources, such as a licensed home health agency, the county IHSS program or the local Area Agency on Aging, as appropriate. The decline is recorded.
If the client is funded by a payer such as a Medi-Cal managed care plan, the Coordinator confirms authorization and any payer assessment requirements before the first visit (SVC-09).

If accepted, the supervisor prepares the service agreement (CR-06) and the service plan (SVC-02) and gives the client the rights notices (CR-01, CR-03). Services do not start until the agreement is signed and a matched aide is available.
The Client Care Supervisor opens the client record (REC-01) with the screening form, assessment, home safety check, emergency contacts, acceptance decision and referral notes.
The Administrator or designee reviews intake and acceptance decisions quarterly as part of quality assurance (GOV-05) to ensure the agency is not accepting clients outside its scope.

responsibilities.duty: Performs the assessment and home safety check, decides on acceptance, makes referrals for skilled needs, and opens the client record.
Checks staff availability, confirms payer authorization and records inquiries.
Reviews denials and unusual acceptances, and ensures intake follows the program description.
Reports to the supervisor any needs or hazards seen that differ from the assessment.
Ensures the program description and intake practices remain consistent.

documentation: Intake Screening Form
Signed assessment and home safety check
Medication-assistance needs record
Emergency contact list
Acceptance or decline decision with reasons and referrals
Payer authorization, if applicable
Quarterly intake review (GOV-05)

policies.title: Service Plan and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: The Client Care Supervisor, affiliated home care aides, the Scheduler/Registry and Billing Coordinator, and the Administrator and designee
policies.purpose: To give each client a written plan that tells the aide exactly what tasks to perform, when, and how, within the limits of non-medical home care, and to keep the plan current.
policies.policy: Every client has a written service plan before the first visit. The plan lists tasks drawn from the home care services in HSC §1796.12(n): bathing, dressing, feeding, exercising, hygiene and grooming, transferring, ambulating, positioning, toileting and incontinence care, assisting with self-administered medication, housekeeping, meals, laundry, transportation, correspondence, phone calls, shopping and companionship. The plan lists the schedule and any transportation. Aides receive the plan before the first visit. As an operator standard, the plan is reviewed at set intervals and when the client's condition changes. Plan changes are signed by the client or representative. The plan never includes tasks outside non-medical home care. These include medication that would otherwise require administration or oversight by a licensed health care professional. The Act sets no plan form, so this process is an operator standard that supports the program description (HCS 281 Section B5) on assignment and supervision.

definitions.definition: The written plan of tasks, schedule, preferences, precautions and transportation for an individual client, based on the assessment (SVC-01).
A written change to the service plan, signed by the client or representative.
A noticeable change in the client's health, function, behavior, home or support that may affect the safety or suitability of the plan (SVC-07).
The tasks on the plan that the aide is permitted to perform for that client. Anything not on the list is not performed without a plan update.

procedures: Within [2] business days after the assessment and before the first visit, the Client Care Supervisor writes the service plan using the agency form and the assessment findings.
The plan lists each authorized task using the terms from HSC §1796.12(n), along with the client's preferences for how and when each task is done, and any precautions the aide needs to know.
The plan states the days, start and end times and frequency of visits, which match the signed service agreement (CR-06).
The plan states any transportation: the purposes, destinations, whether the aide's or client's vehicle is used, and the safety steps in PRG-04.

The plan states how the aide helps with self-administered medication, if at all, within the limits in SVC-04. It says clearly that the aide does not administer medication and does not assist with medication that would otherwise require administration or oversight by a licensed health care professional.
The plan lists emergency contacts, physician, and the steps in an emergency (SVC-07, SAF-04), and any hazards from the home safety check.
The Client Care Supervisor reviews the plan with the client or representative, and the client or representative signs and dates it. A copy is given to the client.

Before the aide's first visit, the Client Care Supervisor gives the plan to the aide and reviews it with the aide in person or by phone. The aide signs or acknowledges receipt, and the date is recorded. The Scheduler does not release a client's schedule to an aide until the acknowledgment is recorded.

Aides perform only the tasks on the plan. If a client asks for a task not on the plan, the aide may do it only if it is a non-medical task and the supervisor has approved it, preferably by plan update beforehand. If the task is outside scope, the aide declines politely and tells the supervisor the same day.

As an operator standard, the Client Care Supervisor reviews each plan with the client at least every 90 days, and during the first 30 days after start of service. The supervisor records the review and signs it.

The supervisor also reviews and updates the plan after any change of condition, hospitalization, fall, change in payer authorization, or at the client's request. A supervisor visit or contact occurs within 2 business days of a reported change of condition.

Plan changes are written on a plan update form. The client or representative signs before the change takes effect. In an urgent situation, the supervisor may start a safe, in-scope change on verbal consent and obtains the signature within 3 business days. The verbal consent is documented.
The supervisor gives the updated plan to the aide and records the acknowledgment. The Coordinator updates the schedule and billing to match the plan.
Outdated plans are marked superseded and kept in the client record (REC-01). Only the current plan is kept in the home.
The Administrator or designee audits a sample of plans quarterly for completeness, in-scope tasks, signatures and timely reviews (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Writes, reviews and updates plans, obtains signatures, briefs aides and keeps plans within scope.
Reads and follows the plan, performs only authorized tasks and reports changes or requests for other tasks.
Aligns the schedule and billing with the current plan and holds schedules until the plan is acknowledged.
Audits plans and resolves scope questions.

documentation: Signed service plan and each signed plan update
Aide acknowledgment of the plan, with date
Plan review records (90-day and event-driven)
Verbal consent notes and follow-up signatures
Quarterly plan audit results

policies.title: Supervision of Caregivers and Supervisory Visits
policies.applies_to: The Client Care Supervisor, Administrator and designee, and all affiliated home care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure aides are assigned and supervised as described in the program description, that client care is observed and documented, and that problems are corrected.
policies.policy: The program description must say how aides are assigned and supervised (HCS 281 Section B5), and this policy carries that out. The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act (HSC §1796.10 et seq.) sets no supervisory-visit frequency and no supervisor-to-aide ratio. The schedule of visits and the caseload standard below are an operator standard of [AGENCY NAME]. The Client Care Supervisor conducts and documents supervisory visits. During visits the supervisor observes aide performance and asks about client satisfaction. Concerns are addressed through corrective action and training.

definitions.definition: A visit by the Client Care Supervisor to the client's home while the aide is present or by arrangement, to observe care, review the service plan and ask the client about satisfaction.
The staff member designated in the program description and lines of supervision chart (JD-02, JD-05) to supervise aides and oversee client care.
A documented step to fix a problem, such as coaching, retraining, schedule change or discipline under PER-09.
A supervisory visit made without telling the aide the time in advance.

procedures: The Administrator or designee assigns each client to a Client Care Supervisor and each aide to a client by the aide's training, language, availability and fit with the service plan. The assignment is recorded on the lines of supervision chart (JD-05) and in the schedule.

As an operator standard, the first supervisory visit takes place within the first 14 days of service. If the aide is new to the client, the supervisor may also make an earlier observation visit or call within the first week.

After the first visit, the supervisor makes a supervisory visit at least every 90 days for each client, and more often if the client's condition is complex, if there have been complaints, or if the aide is new or has a performance concern.

At least [2] of the supervisory visits each year per aide are made while the aide is working, so the supervisor can observe performance directly. Other visits may be made when the aide is not there, if the client agrees, to review the plan with the client.

During each visit the supervisor observes whether the aide: follows the service plan, uses safe transfers and body mechanics, follows infection-control practice (SAF-03), treats the client with dignity, keeps the home safe, handles money under CR-04, and stays within scope (PRG-03).

The supervisor asks the client or representative privately about satisfaction. Topics include whether the aide is on time, respectful and doing the tasks on the plan, and whether the client feels safe. The supervisor asks about any missing items or money concerns.
The supervisor reviews the plan with the client and identifies needed updates (SVC-02). The supervisor also checks the Errand Money Log and EVV or time records for the client (SVC-06).

Within 2 business days after each visit the supervisor completes a Supervisory Visit Report. It records the date, time, who was present, observations, client comments, concerns, and actions taken or planned. The supervisor and the aide sign it, and it is placed in the client record and a copy in the personnel record.

If the supervisor sees an immediate risk to the client, such as unsafe transfers or suspected abuse, the supervisor acts immediately. This means stopping the unsafe practice and arranging emergency help if needed. The supervisor also reports suspected abuse under PER-02 and PRG-05, and tells the Administrator the same day.

For minor concerns, the supervisor coaches the aide on the spot, documents the coaching and sets a follow-up date. For repeated or more serious concerns, the supervisor refers the matter to the Administrator for corrective action under PER-09.
If a concern shows a training gap, the supervisor arranges additional training within [14] days and records it in the training log (TRN-05).
The supervisor follows up on corrective action with another visit or call within [14] days to check that the problem is fixed, and documents the result.

The Administrator or designee reviews each supervisor's caseload monthly. If supervisory visits cannot be completed on schedule, the Administrator adds supervisory staff or reduces new admissions until visits are current.
The supervisor keeps a supervisory visit tracking list showing due dates. The Administrator or designee checks the tracking list monthly to confirm visits are made on time.
Client satisfaction results and corrective actions are summarized quarterly for quality assurance review (GOV-05).

Aides are told at hire and annually that they may be visited at any time, with or without notice, and that they must cooperate and may raise concerns with the supervisor or Administrator without retaliation.

responsibilities.duty: Makes and documents visits, observes aides, asks about satisfaction, coaches, reports abuse concerns and follows up on corrective action.
Cooperates with supervision, follows coaching and training and reports concerns to the supervisor.
Assigns aides and supervisors, monitors caseloads and visit timeliness, and decides formal corrective action.
Supports the schedule so supervisory visits can occur and flags missed or late visits.
Ensures sufficient supervisory staffing.

documentation: Lines of supervision chart (JD-05) and assignment records
Supervisory Visit Reports signed by supervisor and aide
Supervisory visit tracking list
Coaching and corrective action records
Training records for added training (TRN-05)
Monthly caseload review
Quarterly client satisfaction summary (GOV-05)

policies.title: Medication Assistance and Self-Administration Support
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, the Client Care Supervisor, and the Administrator or designee
policies.purpose: To define the limited help with medication that [AGENCY NAME] aides may give, so that clients stay safe and the agency stays within non-medical home care services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides non-medical home care services only. Under HSC §1796.12(n), aides may assist a client only with medication that the client takes by himself or herself (self-administered medication). Aides may not assist with any medication that would otherwise require administration or oversight by a licensed health care professional. Assistance means reminding the client, opening containers, and handing the client the medication. The client takes the medication. Aides do not set up medications, adjust doses, or give injections. Aides document the assistance. They report refusals and errors to the supervisor the same day, or immediately if there is any risk to the client. This policy does not apply to any task that requires a licensed professional. Those tasks are referred to the client's physician, a home health agency, or another licensed provider.

definitions.definition: A medication the client is able to take without another person judging dose, timing, route or technique. The client decides to take it and puts it in or on his or her own body.
Reminding the client that it is time for a medication, opening a bottle or package, and handing the container or the medication to the client. The client takes the medication.
Any medication or treatment that, if the client could not manage it alone, would need administration, calculation, preparation or monitoring by a licensed health care professional.
A missed dose, a dose taken at the wrong time, the wrong medication taken, a duplicate dose, or any other deviation from the client's prescriber instructions that the aide observes or learns about.

procedures: At intake and assessment (SVC-01), the Client Care Supervisor asks whether the client takes medications and whether the client can take them without help from another person. The supervisor records the answer.

The Client Care Supervisor decides whether the client's medication needs fall within self-administration. If the client cannot decide on or take his or her own medication, the supervisor tells the client and representative that the agency cannot provide that help. The supervisor suggests a licensed provider, such as the client's physician or a home health agency, and documents the conversation.
If medication assistance is within scope, the supervisor lists on the service plan (SVC-02) only the permitted tasks: reminders, opening containers, and handing the medication to the client.

During entry-level and annual training (TRN-02, TRN-03), the supervisor or trainer teaches the permitted tasks and the prohibited tasks in this policy. Each aide signs that he or she understands them.
When a medication time arrives, the aide reminds the client. The aide may open the container and hand the medication, as written in the service plan, to the client.
The client takes the medication. The aide does not place it in the client's mouth, push it through a tube, apply it to the client, or guide the client's hand to do so.

The aide does not fill pill organizers, pre-pour or measure doses, crush or split pills, change doses or times, or decide which medication to take. The aide also does not give injections, insulin, inhalers or nebulizer treatments to a client who cannot use them without help, and does not give any other treatment that needs a licensed professional.
The aide does not tell the client to stop, change or skip a medication, and does not give advice about medications. The aide refers questions to the client's pharmacist or prescriber.
If the client refuses a medication, the aide does not insist or hide medication in food. The aide records the refusal and tells the supervisor the same day.

If the aide sees or suspects a medication error, an unusual reaction, or that the client took the wrong medication, the aide acts at once. If the client has trouble breathing, collapses, or is in distress, the aide calls 911, then the supervisor (SVC-07). For other errors, the aide calls the supervisor right away.
The supervisor follows up with the client, representative and, if appropriate, the client's prescriber or pharmacist. The supervisor files an incident report under SAF-02 for any error or reaction.

If an aide is asked to do a prohibited task by the client, a family member or another person, the aide politely declines and tells the supervisor. The supervisor reviews the request, explains the limit to the client and updates the plan if necessary.

The supervisor reviews medication assistance entries during supervisory visits (SVC-03). If aide practice is outside this policy, the supervisor retrains the aide and documents it. Repeated violations are handled under PER-09.
The Administrator reviews medication-related incidents at least quarterly as part of quality assurance (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Provides only reminders, container opening and handing medication to the client; documents each instance; reports refusals, errors and reactions to the supervisor; never does a prohibited task.
Screens at intake and assessment, writes the plan, trains aides, follows up on errors and refusals, reviews entries at supervisory visits.
Ensures this policy is followed, reviews medication incidents, and approves any exception to the scope of services.

documentation: Medication assistance log in the client's record (date, time, medication name as labeled, assistance given, aide initials)
Intake and assessment notes on medication self-administration
Service plan task list
Refusal and error notes and incident reports (SAF-02)
Aide training acknowledgments (TRN-05)
Supervisory visit notes

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Scheduler, registry and billing coordinator; Client Care Supervisor; affiliated home care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure that clients receive scheduled care consistently and that late or missed visits are covered quickly, communicated to the client and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] assigns only affiliated home care aides who are cleared and listed on the Home Care Aide Registry and have completed required training. When an aide is late or absent, the scheduler arranges coverage and notifies the client. Every missed visit and its cause is documented. Backup aides are trained on the client's service plan. Every client receives the agency's after-hours contact number. These are operator standards described in the agency's program description under the HCS 281 application requirements. They are not time limits set by the statute.

definitions.definition: A scheduled visit that does not occur, or does not occur within the window agreed in the service agreement, whether the cause is the aide, the client or other circumstances.
An aide arrives after the scheduled start time. The agency standard is to notify the client when an aide will be more than 15 minutes late.
An affiliated aide who is registry-cleared, trained, and briefed on the client's plan, and is available to cover when the regular aide cannot.
A telephone number, [PHONE], answered by a trained on-call staff member when the office is closed.

procedures: The scheduler assigns an aide to each visit only after confirming in the personnel file that the aide has Live Scan clearance, is on the Home Care Aide Registry, has a current TB clearance and has completed entry-level training (PER-03, PER-04, PER-05, TRN-02).
The scheduler matches the aide to the client by the service plan, language, schedule, location and any client preferences, and records the assignment.

The Client Care Supervisor identifies at least one backup aide for each client and briefs the backup on the service plan, home access, safety concerns and preferences. The supervisor records the briefing.
At the start of service, the scheduler gives the client and representative the office number, business hours and the after-hours contact number, in writing, and records that this was done.
The scheduler confirms the next day's schedule with aides and gives each aide the visit address, hours and plan tasks.

An aide who will be late or cannot work a visit must call the scheduler (or the after-hours number) as soon as the aide knows, and in any event before the visit start time, with the reason and expected arrival time.
For a late arrival of more than 15 minutes, the scheduler calls the client or representative, gives the revised arrival time and offers an alternative if the client prefers.

For an aide absence, the scheduler first contacts the backup aide, then other qualified aides, to cover the full visit. The scheduler confirms the substitute's clearance and briefs the substitute on the plan before the visit.
The scheduler notifies the client or representative of any change of aide before the visit when possible, with the substitute's name and arrival time.

If no coverage can be found, the scheduler tells the client at once, reschedules at the earliest time the client accepts, and notifies the Client Care Supervisor. The supervisor decides if there is a safety risk (for example, a client who cannot be left without care) and arranges a welfare check or contacts family. In an emergency, the aide or supervisor follows SVC-07.

If the aide arrives and the client is not home or does not answer, the aide calls the scheduler. The scheduler tries the client and emergency contacts. If there is any concern for the client's safety, the supervisor follows SVC-07.
The scheduler records every late or missed visit in the missed-visit log the same day: client, date, scheduled time, cause, who was notified and when, how coverage was handled, and follow-up.

The Client Care Supervisor reviews the missed-visit log weekly. If an aide has repeated late or missed visits, the supervisor counsels and documents it under PER-09. If a client has repeated missed visits, the supervisor reviews the schedule and aide match.
The Administrator reviews missed-visit and coverage trends quarterly under GOV-05.
Staff answering the after-hours line record each call, the action taken, and give the call record to the scheduler and supervisor the next business day.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns only cleared and trained aides, arranges coverage, notifies clients, keeps the missed-visit log and gives clients the after-hours number.
Identifies and briefs backup aides, assesses client safety when care is missed, reviews the log weekly and corrects aide performance.
Arrives on time, calls the scheduler before a late or missed visit, and follows the backup and notification steps.
Ensures staffing and on-call coverage and reviews trends for quality assurance.

documentation: Schedule and assignment records
Verification of aide clearance and registry status at assignment
Missed-visit and late-visit log
Backup aide briefing record
Record of after-hours number given to client
After-hours call log
Counseling notes (personnel file)

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: Scheduler, registry and billing coordinator; Client Care Supervisor; affiliated home care aides; Administrator or designee
policies.purpose: To record the actual start and stop time of every visit, to meet electronic visit verification requirements for Medi-Cal-funded personal care services, and to support accurate pay and billing.
policies.policy: Electronic visit verification (EVV) is required for Medicaid (Medi-Cal) personal care services under 42 U.S.C. §1396b(l). It applies only to Medi-Cal-funded visits and does not apply to private-pay visits. Before providing any Medi-Cal-funded service, [AGENCY NAME] will confirm with DHCS or the client's managed care plan which EVV system and data elements are required. For all clients, regardless of payer, aides record actual start and stop times, including travel time between clients, and the agency reviews and corrects exceptions with a documented reason. As a third-party employer of home care workers, [AGENCY NAME] may not claim the companionship or live-in exemptions from minimum wage and overtime (29 CFR §552.109), so accurate time records are the basis of wage-hour compliance (PER-07).

definitions.definition: An electronic system that records the date of service, type of service, client, aide, and the start and end time and location of a visit, for Medi-Cal-funded personal care services.
A visit record that is missing information or does not match the schedule or authorization, such as a missing clock-in or clock-out, a late arrival, a location mismatch or a manual entry.
The real time the aide began and ended work, not the scheduled time.
Time an aide spends traveling between clients during the work day, which is working time.

procedures: Before accepting a Medi-Cal-funded client, the Administrator or designee confirms in writing with DHCS or the client's managed care plan whether EVV is required for the service and which EVV system, data elements and submission method the payer requires. The confirmation is kept in the payer file.
The scheduler flags each client's payer in the scheduling system so Medi-Cal visits are identified for EVV and private-pay visits are not.

The Client Care Supervisor or scheduler trains each aide on how to clock in and out, including the steps for the payer-required EVV system, before the aide's first visit. The training is recorded (TRN-05).

For every visit, the aide records the actual start time on arrival and the actual stop time on departure, in the system the agency uses. Private-pay visits are timed in the agency's timekeeping system.

The aide records travel time between clients as working time, with the start and stop times of each trip. Commute from home to the first client and from the last client to home is handled under PER-07.

An aide who cannot clock in or out (for example, no signal or a device fault) calls the scheduler during the visit. The scheduler records the details, and the aide enters the actual times as soon as the system allows.
The aide never records time for work not done, never clocks in or out for another person, and never alters a time record. Violations are handled under PER-09 and GOV-06.
The scheduler runs an exception report each business day for the previous day's visits.

For each exception, the scheduler contacts the aide, and the client if needed, to find out what happened, and corrects the record only to reflect what actually happened. Each correction is entered with the reason, the person correcting and the date.
The Client Care Supervisor reviews exceptions weekly for patterns, such as repeated late arrivals or short visits, and follows up with the aide under SVC-05 and PER-09.
Before each payroll run, the billing coordinator reconciles aide time records with the schedule and reviews overtime hours. Differences are resolved before pay is issued (PER-07).

Before billing a payer, the billing coordinator confirms that Medi-Cal visits have verified EVV records that match the authorization and the claim. Visits that do not match are held until corrected or not billed (GOV-06).
The Administrator or designee reviews a sample of time records, exceptions and corrections quarterly and reports results under GOV-05.
Time and EVV records are kept as part of payroll and client records (PER-06, REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Records actual start, stop and travel times for every visit, reports system failures at once and never falsifies time.
Confirms EVV requirements, runs daily exception reports, documents corrections, reconciles time with payroll and billing.
Trains aides on timekeeping, reviews exceptions for patterns and corrects aide performance.
Confirms the payer's EVV system, oversees wage-hour compliance and audits time records.

documentation: Written confirmation of EVV requirements from DHCS or managed care plan
EVV and timekeeping records (start, stop, travel)
Daily exception reports and correction log with reasons
Aide timekeeping training records
Payroll reconciliation records
Quarterly audit results

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, the Client Care Supervisor, the scheduler and the Administrator or designee
policies.purpose: To make sure aides respond correctly to an emergency or a change in a client's condition, stay within non-medical scope, and report promptly so the service plan is updated.
policies.policy: Entry-level safety training required by HSC §1796.44(b) covers emergency procedures, and each aide completes it before being alone with a client. In any emergency, the aide calls 911 first, then the supervisor. Because home care services are non-medical (HSC §1796.12(n)), aides give no medical treatment beyond first aid. Any change in a client's condition is reported to the supervisor the same day, the service plan is updated, and an incident report is completed (SAF-02).

definitions.definition: A situation that threatens life, health or safety, such as chest pain, trouble breathing, stroke signs, unresponsiveness, a serious fall or injury, severe bleeding, choking, fire, or a suspected overdose.

Any new or worsening change in a client's physical, mental, emotional or functional state or behavior, such as a fall, new confusion, loss of appetite, new pain, skin changes, new difficulty with transfers, or a change in mood.
Immediate basic care given until professional help arrives, within the aide's entry-level safety training.

procedures: During entry-level training (TRN-02), the trainer teaches each aide the emergency procedures in this policy, how to call 911, how to give basic first aid within training, and how to report. The aide's completion is recorded (TRN-05).

At intake (SVC-01), the supervisor records the client's emergency contacts, physician, known conditions, allergies and any advance directive or preferences the client or representative wishes to share. A copy is available to the aide at the home or through the office.
In an emergency, the aide calls 911 immediately. The aide gives the address, the client's name and what has happened, and stays with the client.

The aide gives first aid within training only, and does not give medication, food or drink, or treatment, other than what first aid allows. The aide does not move a client with a suspected fall injury unless there is immediate danger.

After calling 911, the aide calls the supervisor or the after-hours number, [PHONE], and then the client's emergency contact or representative. If the aide cannot reach the supervisor, the aide continues to attend to the client and leaves a message.

The aide gives emergency responders the client's medication list and emergency information if available, and does not leave the client until responders take over. If the client is taken to the hospital, the aide gives the supervisor the hospital name.

For a non-emergency change in condition, the aide tells the client's supervisor the same day, by phone if serious or by the agency's reporting method if not. The aide describes what was seen, when it began and what the client said, without diagnosing.

The supervisor reviews each report the same day it is received, contacts the client or representative, and decides whether to recommend a call to the client's physician or other licensed provider. The supervisor may also arrange an extra visit or a supervisory visit.
If the client's needs now exceed non-medical services, the supervisor discusses referrals with the client and representative (SVC-08).
The supervisor updates the service plan after any change in condition, tells all aides assigned to the client about the update, and records the date and who was informed (SVC-02).

The aide or supervisor completes an incident report under SAF-02 for every emergency, injury, fall or significant change in condition, by the end of the shift or by the next business day if the aide is unable to complete it sooner.
If the incident involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member also follows PER-02 and PRG-05 and does not wait for the incident report.
The supervisor makes any required reports to the state under REC-02 and notifies the Administrator the same day of any serious event, including death, serious injury or 911 transport.
The Administrator reviews emergencies and changes in condition quarterly, looking for patterns that call for plan changes or more training (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Calls 911 in any emergency, then the supervisor; gives first aid only; reports changes in condition the same day; completes the incident report.
Reviews reports the same day, contacts the client, representative or provider as needed, updates the plan and informs aides, ensures incident reports are completed.
Provides after-hours coverage and notifies the supervisor of any call about an emergency or change in condition.
Is notified of serious events, makes required state reports and reviews trends.

documentation: Emergency training record (TRN-05)
Client emergency contact and information sheet
Change-in-condition notes
Incident reports (SAF-02)
Service plan updates (SVC-02)
After-hours call log
Reports to the state, if any (REC-02)

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Discontinuation of Services
policies.applies_to: Administrator or designee, Client Care Supervisor, scheduler and affiliated home care aides
policies.purpose: To ensure that the end of services is planned, communicated in writing, safe for the client, and documented.
policies.policy: The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act (HSC §1796.10 et seq.) sets no specific discharge rule for home care organizations. This policy is an operator standard of [AGENCY NAME]. Before services end for any reason the agency gives the client or representative written notice with the reasons and a transition plan. The agency makes safety referrals when the client's care needs exceed non-medical services. The agency notifies the family or representative and, if the payer is involved, the payer. The agency documents the discharge and keeps the record under REC-01.

definitions.definition: The end of all services to a client, whether started by the client, the representative or the agency.
The move of a client's care to another provider or setting, such as another agency, a home health agency, assisted living or a skilled nursing facility.
A written plan for the end of service that lists the last date, referrals, handoff of information the client authorizes, and any open safety concerns.

procedures: Services may end when: the client or representative asks; the client no longer needs services; care needs exceed non-medical home care; the client moves, is hospitalized or admitted to a facility, or dies; payment or authorization ends; the home is unsafe for aides or the client or others endanger aides; the client violates the service agreement; or the agency cannot staff the service.
The Client Care Supervisor discusses any proposed agency-initiated discharge with the Administrator before the client is told. The Administrator approves it in writing and records the reason.

For a client request, the supervisor confirms the request, the last day of service and any final concerns, and documents it. Services end on the date the client chooses, and the client is told of any amounts owed for services provided under the service agreement (CR-06).

For an agency-initiated discharge, the supervisor gives the client and representative written notice at least 14 days before the last day of service, stating the reason, the last date, how to ask questions or file a grievance (CR-02), and the transition plan. A shorter notice is allowed only if there is an immediate safety threat to the client or staff, or the client's need for a higher level of care cannot wait. The reason is documented.

The supervisor reviews the client's needs and, if they exceed non-medical services, makes referrals to the client's physician, a home health agency, hospice, adult day or other licensed or community services, and gives the client a list of options. The supervisor documents each referral.

If the client may be unsafe without care, the supervisor works with the family or representative on a safety plan and does not end services until the client has been told of the risks and has been given referrals. If the supervisor believes the client is in danger of abuse or neglect, the supervisor follows PER-02 and PRG-05.

The supervisor notifies the family or representative named in the record of the discharge, with the client's permission as needed under CR-03, and notifies the payer, including a managed care plan, if the payer is involved (SVC-09).

With a signed release, the supervisor sends the receiving provider the client's service plan summary and relevant information. Information is not released without client authorization except as law requires (CR-03).
The scheduler cancels future visits, tells the assigned aides, and makes sure any final visits are covered (SVC-05).
The aide returns or accounts for client keys, access codes and any property, and the supervisor records it (CR-04).
The billing coordinator issues the final billing statement and refunds any prepaid amount owed under the service agreement within the time stated in the agreement (CR-06).
The supervisor completes a discharge summary within [7] days after the last visit, stating the reason, the date, the notice given, referrals and the client's status at discharge.
If the client dies, the supervisor records the date and circumstances, notifies the Administrator, and completes any incident report under SAF-02 and any state report under REC-02.
The Administrator reviews discharges quarterly, especially agency-initiated ones, for patterns and for quality improvement (GOV-05). The client record is closed and retained under REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Approves agency-initiated discharges, reviews notices and trends, and ensures required reports are made.
Gives written notice, develops the transition plan, makes referrals, notifies family and payer, writes the discharge summary.
Cancels visits, informs aides, issues final billing and refunds.
Reports client or family requests to end service, returns keys and property, and continues care through the last date.

documentation: Client or representative request to end services
Administrator approval and reason for agency-initiated discharge
Written discharge notice and transition plan
Referral list and record of referrals
Notices to family, representative and payer
Release of information
Discharge summary
Final billing and refund record

policies.title: Coordination with Medi-Cal Programs and Other Payers
policies.applies_to: Administrator or designee, scheduler and billing coordinator, Client Care Supervisor
policies.purpose: To describe how [AGENCY NAME] works with Medi-Cal programs and other payers accurately, and to avoid billing for or promising services that the agency is not authorized to provide.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a licensed Home Care Organization providing non-medical home care. In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) pays individual providers, not agencies, and IHSS providers are not home care organizations under HSC §1796.17. Personal Care and Homemaker Services (PCHS) is a Community Support offered by Medi-Cal managed care plans. The plans contract with and pay providers, and the agency may bill a plan for PCHS only under a contract with that plan. The DHCS pricing resource for PCHS ($29 low, $33 midpoint, $38 high per hour) is non-binding. Rates are those negotiated with each plan. An HCO that is not enrolled for the Home and Community-Based Alternatives (HCBA) Waiver is not covered by the Personal Care Agency exemption from licensure. Federal HCBS settings rules (42 CFR §441.301(c) and §441.710) apply only to services funded through HCBA or other Medicaid HCBS programs. EVV applies to Medi-Cal visits (42 U.S.C. §1396b(l); see SVC-06). The agency does not bill any payer until it has a contract or authorization on file.

definitions.definition: In-Home Supportive Services, a county-administered, consumer-directed program that pays individual providers through state payroll. It does not pay agencies.
A Community Support offered by Medi-Cal managed care plans under DHCS policy. Plans contract with and pay providers.
The DHCS Home and Community-Based Alternatives Waiver, which covers Waiver Personal Care Services. Medi-Cal Personal Care Agencies providing HCBA Waiver services are exempt from HCO licensure.
A Medi-Cal health plan that authorizes services, contracts with providers and pays claims.
Services paid by the client or family directly, or by long-term care insurance, under the service agreement (CR-06).

procedures: At intake (SVC-01), the supervisor asks each client how services will be paid: private pay, long-term care insurance, a Medi-Cal managed care plan, or another source. The supervisor records the answer.

If a client or family asks about IHSS, the supervisor explains that IHSS is run by the county, pays individual providers, and is not provided by the agency. The supervisor gives the county IHSS contact and does not tell the client to leave or stay in IHSS. The agency does not hold itself out as an IHSS provider.

If a client has Medi-Cal managed care and wants PCHS, the billing coordinator confirms with the plan that the agency is a contracted provider, that the client is eligible and that the service is authorized, in what amount and for what dates, before the first visit. The authorization is filed in the client's payer record.

The Administrator or designee decides whether to contract with managed care plans. Rates are negotiated with each plan. The DHCS benchmark of $29, $33 and $38 per hour is a reference only, and the agency is bound only by the rate in its signed contract.

The Administrator confirms that the agency's HCO license is current and that staff, training and supervision meet the plan's contract requirements before beginning services. Any plan conditions are added to this manual under GOV-04.

The agency does not provide or bill HCBA Waiver services unless the agency is enrolled for the waiver. The HCO license does not authorize the agency to claim the Personal Care Agency exemption, and the Administrator verifies enrollment with DHCS before any HCBA services are offered.

If the agency is enrolled in the HCBA Waiver or another Medicaid HCBS program, the Administrator confirms the program's settings and person-centered service planning requirements (42 CFR §441.301(c); §441.710 where applicable) and adds them to the service plan process (SVC-02). These requirements are not applied to private-pay clients.
For Medi-Cal-funded visits, the scheduler follows SVC-06, including confirming the required EVV system with DHCS or the managed care plan.

The Client Care Supervisor delivers services only as authorized by the payer's authorization and the service plan. If the client's needs change, the supervisor asks the plan to reauthorize and does not provide extra services without approval, unless there is an emergency (SVC-07).

The billing coordinator bills the payer only for services delivered, as verified by time records and EVV, within the authorization, and with the plan's required documentation (GOV-06). Errors found after billing are corrected and any overpayment is refunded promptly.
The supervisor notifies the plan of discharge, hospitalization, change of address, death or any change affecting authorization (SVC-08).
The supervisor shares client information with a payer only as permitted by the plan contract, the law and the client's authorization (CR-03).
The Administrator keeps a current list of contracted payers, contacts, authorization requirements and plan audit requirements, and updates it at least once a year.
The Administrator reviews payer denials, audits and complaints, and the results are reported under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Decides on payer contracts, confirms licensure and enrollment status, signs contracts and oversees compliance and audits.
Verifies authorizations before service, schedules and bills only authorized services, runs EVV for Medi-Cal visits, corrects billing errors.
Identifies payer at intake, explains program differences to clients, keeps services within authorization, tells the plan about changes.

documentation: Payer source recorded at intake
Managed care plan contracts and rate sheets
Authorizations and eligibility verification
DHCS enrollment confirmation for any HCBA Waiver services
EVV records for Medi-Cal visits
Billing and claim records
Payer correspondence and audit files
Current list of contracted payers

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention
policies.applies_to: All owners, the Administrator and designee, the Client Care Supervisor, schedulers, affiliated home care aides, volunteers and anyone else with contact with clients of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To prevent, detect and respond to abuse, neglect, abandonment, isolation, abduction and financial exploitation of clients. This policy sets out the preventive measures [AGENCY NAME] takes. The reporting steps are in PRG-05 and PER-02.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect or exploitation of any client by staff, family members, visitors or anyone else. Anyone with full or intermittent responsibility for the care of an elder or dependent adult, paid or unpaid, is a mandated reporter under WIC §15630. Aides are therefore mandated reporters. As the licensee, [AGENCY NAME] must also report suspected or known abuse of a dependent adult, elder or child as required by WIC §15630 and the Penal Code child abuse reporting provisions (Penal Code §§11164-11174.3), and must keep a copy of each report for review by CDSS (HSC §1796.42(e)). Prevention has four parts. First, aides are cleared and trained before any client contact. Second, aides are trained every year on how to report, prevent and detect abuse and neglect (HSC §1796.44). Third, supervision and client contact are used to detect problems early. Fourth, every allegation is answered immediately and documented. As an operator standard, [AGENCY NAME] removes an accused aide from the client while the allegation is reviewed. This policy does not replace the duty to report. Reporting does not depend on the agency's own review, and no one may delay or block a report.

definitions.definition: A person with full or intermittent responsibility for the care or custody of an elder or dependent adult, whether or not paid, who must report observed, known or reasonably suspected abuse (WIC §15630(a)).

definitions.term: Abuse and neglect (as listed in WIC §15630(b)(1))
definitions.definition: Physical abuse, abandonment, abduction, isolation, financial abuse or neglect of an elder or dependent adult.
Taking, using or misdirecting a client's money or property, including gifts, loans, bank cards, checks or account access, without the client's informed consent or by pressure.
An aide who has completed the background check and registry clearance, has met the pre-service requirements in PER-03 and PER-04, and has completed entry-level training.

procedures: Before scheduling any client contact, the Administrator or designee confirms that the aide has completed the clearance, registry and Live Scan steps in PER-03 and PER-04. No aide is placed with a client until this is documented in the personnel file.

Before any client contact, the aide completes the 5-hour entry-level training in TRN-02 (2 hours of orientation and 3 hours of safety). Orientation includes [AGENCY NAME]'s zero-tolerance rule and the duty to report.

Each year, the aide completes the 5-hour annual training in TRN-03. It must cover how to report, prevent and detect abuse and neglect, and clients' rights and safety (HSC §1796.44). The training is recorded in the training log (TRN-05).
Each aide signs an acknowledgment at hire and each year that he or she understands the mandated-reporter duty and the reporting steps in PRG-05 and PER-02.

Aides follow the boundaries in PER-08 and CR-04. They do not borrow money, accept large gifts, handle client bank cards or checks, act as agent for the client, or use client property for personal purposes.

The Client Care Supervisor reviews each client's care during supervisory visits (SVC-03). The supervisor watches for warning signs: unexplained injuries, weight loss, poor hygiene, fear of an aide, sudden changes in finances, missing property, or isolation from family.

During intake and at each reassessment, the supervisor tells the client and family how to reach the supervisor and the Administrator with concerns (CR-02). The client's rights notice (CR-01) states that the client may report concerns to the agency and to outside agencies.

Any staff member who sees, suspects or is told of abuse, neglect or exploitation follows PRG-05 and PER-02 immediately. For a dependent adult or elder, the person makes the telephone or confidential internet report immediately or as soon as practicably possible, and the written or internet report follows within 2 working days (WIC §15630(b)(1)). For abuse outside a long-term care facility, the report goes to adult protective services or local law enforcement.
If a client is in immediate danger, the staff member calls 911 first, stays with the client if safe to do so, and then notifies the Client Care Supervisor.
The Client Care Supervisor or Administrator responds to every allegation immediately, including anonymous ones and those that seem unlikely. The response is not postponed to the next business day.

When the allegation involves an aide of [AGENCY NAME], the Administrator removes that aide from the client pending review. This is an operator standard. The removal is neutral, does not assume guilt, and is documented. The aide has no contact with the client or the client's family about the allegation during review.

The Administrator arranges safe replacement care so that the client is not left without services, and tells the client and the client's representative what was done, unless law enforcement or APS asks otherwise.

[AGENCY NAME] cooperates fully with APS, law enforcement and CDSS. The Administrator does not interfere with, discourage or retaliate against anyone who reports. Retaliation is grounds for discipline (PER-09).

The Administrator keeps a copy of every suspected-abuse report made by [AGENCY NAME] or its aides, and keeps them available to CDSS during normal business hours (HSC §1796.42(e)). The copies are kept in a secure abuse-report file separate from routine client records.

The Administrator completes an incident record under SAF-02 for each allegation. It records what happened, the date and time, who was told, the report made and the follow-up. The Administrator also records the outcome of the agency's review and any discipline or separation (PER-09, PER-10).

The Administrator reviews all abuse-related events at least quarterly under GOV-05. The review looks for patterns by aide, client, time or location, and for training or supervision gaps. Findings are recorded and corrective action is taken.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces zero tolerance, removes accused aides pending review, keeps copies of all abuse reports, cooperates with outside agencies, and reviews trends.
Detects warning signs at supervisory visits, responds immediately to every allegation, arranges replacement care, and completes incident documentation.
Does not schedule uncleared or untrained aides and does not assign an aide who is removed pending review.
Completes training, follows boundaries, and reports observed, known or suspected abuse as required by WIC §15630 and PRG-05.

documentation: Clearance and registry confirmation (PER-03, PER-04) before client contact
Entry-level and annual training records (TRN-02, TRN-03, TRN-05)
Signed mandated-reporter acknowledgments
Copy of each suspected-abuse report in the abuse-report file
Incident record and review notes (SAF-02)
Record of removal of the aide pending review, and its outcome
Quarterly review minutes (GOV-05)

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, the Client Care Supervisor, schedulers, the Administrator and any other staff of [AGENCY NAME] who witness or learn of an incident
policies.purpose: To make sure incidents involving clients, staff or property are reported, documented, followed up and reviewed for patterns, and to keep these reports separate from, and consistent with, the mandatory abuse-reporting process.
policies.policy: The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act (HSC §1796.10 et seq.) does not set a general incident-report form or deadline. [AGENCY NAME] has therefore adopted its own incident reporting system as an operator standard. Aides report falls, injuries and property loss to the Client Care Supervisor the same day. The supervisor completes an incident form and follows up. The Administrator reviews incident trends under GOV-05. Abuse reports have their own deadlines. A suspected abuse report under WIC §15630 is made by telephone or confidential internet tool immediately or as soon as practicably possible, and the written or internet report follows within 2 working days. A copy of each abuse report is kept and available to CDSS during normal business hours (HSC §1796.42(e)). The internal incident process never delays or replaces an abuse report. An incident form does not discharge any individual's own duty to report.

definitions.definition: Any unexpected event that harms or could harm a client, aide or other person, or that involves loss or damage of property. Examples: a fall, injury, medical emergency, 911 call, missed visit that puts a client at risk, missing property, a client's complaint about an aide, a vehicle accident while transporting a client, workplace violence, or an exposure to blood or body fluids.
Before the end of the aide's shift or, for events after hours, by telephone to the on-call supervisor immediately, with the written form completed by the end of the next business day.
[AGENCY NAME]'s standard form recording the date, time, place, people involved, description, immediate action, notifications and follow-up.

procedures: The aide first makes sure the client and anyone else involved is safe. If there is an emergency, the aide calls 911 and follows SVC-07, then calls the Client Care Supervisor or the on-call line at [PHONE].
The aide reports every fall, injury and property loss to the Client Care Supervisor the same day, even if the client seems unhurt or does not want a report made.

If the incident could be abuse, neglect or exploitation, the aide follows PRG-05 and PER-02 at once. The reporting deadlines in WIC §15630 apply from that moment. The aide does not wait for the supervisor's review before reporting.
The aide writes down the facts on the visit note or on a written statement the same day. The aide records only what he or she saw, heard and did, without speculation or blame.

The Client Care Supervisor completes the incident form within one business day of notice, using the aide's statement and any other information. The form records who was notified, including the client's representative or emergency contact where appropriate.
The supervisor contacts the client, or the client's representative, within one business day to check on the client's condition and explain what is being done.

For falls and injuries, the supervisor decides whether the service plan or the aide's instructions must change, and arranges a reassessment or plan update under SVC-02 if so. If the client's condition has changed, the supervisor follows SVC-07.

For property loss or damage, the supervisor follows CR-04: she asks the client or representative what is missing, checks with the aide and others who had access, and documents the findings. If theft or financial exploitation is suspected, the supervisor treats it as possible abuse under PRG-05.
For an aide's work-related injury, the supervisor follows SAF-05 and the workers' compensation process in addition to completing the incident form.
For a client complaint about care or an aide, the supervisor also opens a complaint record under CR-02.

The supervisor gives the completed incident form to the Administrator within two business days of the event. The Administrator reviews it for completeness, required notifications and corrective action, and signs it.

If a report to an outside agency is needed (such as APS, law enforcement, or CDSS under REC-02), the Administrator makes sure it is made and that a copy is filed. Copies of abuse reports are kept in the abuse-report file under SAF-01.

Incident forms are filed in a confidential incident log. Information that identifies the client is also placed in the client record (REC-01). Personnel actions arising from an incident go in the personnel file (PER-06), not in the client record.

The Administrator reviews the incident log at least quarterly under GOV-05. The review looks at types of incident, frequency, aide, client, time of day and location, and sets corrective actions such as retraining, supervision changes or plan changes.
Staff who report incidents in good faith are not disciplined for reporting. Failure to report an incident the same day is a performance issue handled under PER-09.

responsibilities.duty: Secures safety, calls 911 when needed, reports falls, injuries and property loss to the supervisor the same day, and documents facts.
Completes the incident form, contacts the client, follows up, updates the service plan if needed, and sends the form to the Administrator.
Reviews and signs each form, ensures outside reports are made and filed, and reviews trends quarterly under GOV-05.
Takes after-hours calls, reaches the on-call supervisor, and logs the time of each call.

documentation: Incident form signed by the supervisor and Administrator
Aide's written statement or visit note
Incident log (confidential)
Copy of any abuse report made (kept per SAF-01)
Record of client or representative contact and follow-up
Service plan update, if any (SVC-02)
Quarterly trend review (GOV-05)

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, the Client Care Supervisor, schedulers and anyone else of [AGENCY NAME] who enters a client's home or office areas
policies.purpose: To reduce the spread of infection among clients and staff by training, tuberculosis screening, hand hygiene, protective equipment, exposure response and exclusion of ill staff.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] protects clients and staff from infection. Entry-level safety training of at least 3 hours includes infection control and is completed before the aide is present with a client (HSC §1796.44). Each aide has a tuberculosis examination as a condition of initial and continuing employment (HSC §1796.45). Aides use hand hygiene before and after client care and wear gloves for personal care. [AGENCY NAME] provides gloves and other personal protective equipment at no cost to the aide.
