Aides provide non-medical care, but where the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) applies, [AGENCY NAME] also provides the required protections and a sharps and exposure procedure. As a precaution even if the standard may not apply, the exposure steps below are followed for any contact with blood or body fluids. Staff with symptoms of a contagious illness do not work with clients.

definitions.definition: Gloves, masks, gowns, eye protection or other items that protect the aide and the client from contact with infectious material.
Basic practices applied to every client: hand hygiene, gloves for contact with body fluids, safe handling of soiled items and laundry, and cleaning of surfaces.
Contact of an aide's eyes, mouth, broken skin or other mucous membranes with blood or other potentially infectious material, or a needlestick or sharps injury.
The licensed medical practitioner's certificate documenting the aide's tuberculosis examination and result, which the aide submits and [AGENCY NAME] keeps on file (HSC §1796.45(d)).

procedures: Before any client contact, each aide completes the safety portion of entry-level training (at least 3 hours), which includes infection control (TRN-02). The training is recorded in the training log (TRN-05). Infection control is refreshed in annual training (TRN-03) as needed.

TB examination. Each aide hired on or after January 1, 2016 has a TB examination within 90 days before employment or within 7 days after the hire date. The exam is a CDC-recommended, FDA-licensed TB infection test and, if the result is positive, a chest X-ray (HSC §1796.45(a)-(b)).
The aide submits the practitioner's certificate after each exam, and the Administrator or designee files it in the personnel file (PER-05, PER-06) (HSC §1796.45(d)).

If the aide's test is positive, the aide does not work with clients unless [AGENCY NAME] has documentation from a licensed medical professional that the aide poses no risk of spreading disease (HSC §1796.45(b)).

A negative-result aide repeats the exam at least every 2 years. After a positive test has been followed by an X-ray, repeat exams are no longer required (HSC §1796.45(c)). The designee keeps a tracking list and notifies each aide 60 days before the exam is due.

For a transferring aide, [AGENCY NAME] accepts a certificate from within the past 2 years, or written verification from the prior home care organization that it holds the certificate, with a copy provided before the aide starts (HSC §1796.45(f)).

An aide who does not complete a required TB exam by the due date is removed from the schedule until the exam is documented, because the exam is a condition of initial and continuing employment (HSC §1796.45(e)).

Aides perform hand hygiene (washing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, or alcohol-based rub if hands are not visibly soiled) on arrival, before and after personal care, after contact with body fluids, after removing gloves, before preparing food and before leaving.
Aides wear disposable gloves for personal care and any contact with body fluids or soiled items, and change them between tasks and between clients. They never reuse disposable gloves.
[AGENCY NAME] supplies PPE, including gloves, masks and cleaning supplies, and replaces stock at the aide's request. The Scheduler or designee checks each aide's supplies at least monthly.

Aides bag soiled linens and waste, clean and disinfect surfaces after personal care, and do not handle needles or sharps. If a client uses sharps, the aide does not recap, bend or dispose of them, and tells the supervisor.

After any exposure incident, the aide immediately washes the area with soap and water (or flushes eyes and mouth with water), then calls the Client Care Supervisor. The supervisor tells the aide to see a medical provider promptly, completes an incident form (SAF-02), and starts a workers' compensation claim (SAF-05).

If the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard applies to any job classification at [AGENCY NAME], the Administrator confirms with counsel or a safety consultant and sets up the required exposure control plan, training, and medical follow-up for those classifications.

An aide with fever, vomiting, diarrhea, a persistent cough, a rash of unknown cause or another sign of a contagious illness does not work with clients and tells the Scheduler before the shift. The aide returns after symptoms resolve or after a medical provider clears him or her. The Scheduler arranges replacement care (SVC-05).

If a client has a known or suspected contagious illness, the aide tells the supervisor, who decides on added precautions and whether other aides or the client's medical provider should be told. Client information is shared only as permitted by CR-03.
The Administrator reviews infection-related incidents and exposure reports at least quarterly under GOV-05 and updates this policy as public health guidance changes.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures TB compliance, supplies PPE, reviews exposures and decides whether the OSHA bloodborne standard applies.
Directs precautions for clients with contagious illness, responds to exposures and follows up on incident forms.
Tracks TB due dates, keeps PPE available and removes ill or non-compliant aides from the schedule.
Completes training and TB exams, follows hand hygiene and PPE practices, reports exposures and symptoms.

documentation: Training records showing infection control (TRN-02, TRN-03, TRN-05)
TB certificate and exam date for each aide (PER-05, PER-06)
TB due-date tracking list
Documentation of no risk of spreading disease for any aide with a positive test
Incident form and workers' compensation claim for each exposure (SAF-02, SAF-05)
PPE supply log
Record of ill-staff exclusions and return dates

policies.title: Client Emergency and Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, Client Care Supervisor, schedulers, affiliated home care aides and all other staff of [AGENCY NAME] involved in client care or scheduling
policies.purpose: To prepare each client, and [AGENCY NAME] itself, for medical emergencies and disasters such as wildfire, earthquake, flood, power outage or extreme heat, and to restore contact and service quickly afterward.
policies.policy: The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act (HSC §1796.10 et seq.) does not contain an emergency-plan rule. [AGENCY NAME] adopts this policy as an operator standard. Entry-level safety training covers emergency procedures, and every aide completes it before client contact (HSC §1796.44). [AGENCY NAME] prepares an individual emergency plan for each client with contacts, evacuation help needed and a current medication list. After a disaster, it contacts high-risk clients first. It keeps a backup way to schedule care and communicate with staff and clients if normal systems fail. Aides do not provide medical care in an emergency. They call 911, give basic safety help within their training, and notify the supervisor.

definitions.definition: A one-page plan for each client listing emergency contacts, medical provider, pharmacy, evacuation needs, equipment such as oxygen or mobility aids, pets, and a current medication list.

A client who cannot evacuate or call for help alone, lives alone, depends on electrically powered equipment, has dementia or a serious medical condition, or has no reliable family or neighbor support.
Any event such as wildfire, earthquake, flood, severe weather, widespread power or communications loss, or public-health emergency that disrupts normal services in the area served (PRG-06).

procedures: At intake, the Client Care Supervisor completes an emergency plan for the client with the client or representative (SVC-01). It lists emergency contacts, the physician, preferred hospital, pharmacy, evacuation help needed, equipment needing power, pets, and the client's address with directions in case of a 911 call.

The supervisor attaches a current medication list to the plan, taken from the client or family. The aide does not manage medications beyond SVC-04. The list is updated at each reassessment and whenever the client reports a change.
The supervisor rates each client as high-risk or standard and records the rating in the client record (REC-01). The supervisor reviews the plan at every reassessment and at least every six months.
The aide keeps a copy of the plan available in the home (or on the aide's approved mobile app) and reviews it on the first visit and after each update.
Before working alone with a client, every aide completes emergency procedures training as part of the 3-hour safety portion of entry-level training (TRN-02). Annual training refreshes it (TRN-03).

In a medical emergency, the aide calls 911 first, gives the dispatcher the address and the client's condition, stays with the client, follows dispatcher instructions, then calls the supervisor. The aide gives responders the medication list. SVC-07 and SAF-02 apply.

In a fire, earthquake, flood or evacuation order, the aide helps the client leave safely if it can be done safely, follows local evacuation orders, brings the emergency plan and medication list, and calls the supervisor from a safe place. The aide does not put himself or herself at serious risk.

Before a forecast event such as a red-flag fire warning, a heat wave or a storm, the Administrator or supervisor calls each high-risk client or representative to confirm the plan, supplies and the transport or contact person.

As soon as it is safe after a disaster, the Administrator activates the disaster plan. The supervisor contacts every high-risk client by phone, text, in person or through an emergency contact. Contact with all high-risk clients is attempted first, followed by all remaining clients. Each attempt and result is recorded.

The Scheduler contacts each scheduled aide to check on safety and availability. The Scheduler rearranges visits so high-risk clients are covered first (SVC-05) and tells clients about changes in service.

If a client cannot be reached, the supervisor asks the emergency contact to check on the client. If there is no response and a concern remains, the supervisor requests a welfare check from local law enforcement or fire services.

[AGENCY NAME] keeps a backup way to schedule and communicate: a printed or offline copy of the schedule and the client and aide contact list, updated weekly, a secondary phone line or mobile phone [PHONE], and a designated alternate location for operations if the office at [ADDRESS] is not usable.
The Administrator keeps the printed contact list and on-call roster in a secure location off-site and with the Client Care Supervisor.

If services must be reduced or paused because of a disaster, the supervisor tells each affected client or representative as soon as possible, records the change and resumes services as soon as safe. Any lasting discontinuation follows SVC-08.
After each disaster or drill, the Administrator reviews what worked and what did not under GOV-05 and revises the plan. All staff are told of any changes.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the agency disaster plan and backup systems, activates the plan, and reviews performance afterward.
Completes and updates client emergency plans, rates risk, contacts high-risk clients after a disaster.
Keeps the offline schedule and contact lists, reassigns visits and contacts aides after a disaster.
Knows the client's plan, calls 911 in emergencies, helps with safe evacuation, and reports to the supervisor.

documentation: Individual client emergency plan and medication list (REC-01)
Risk rating for each client
Entry-level and annual emergency-procedure training records (TRN-05)
Disaster contact log with each attempt and outcome
Updated offline schedule and contact list
After-action review (GOV-05)

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All affiliated home care aides, the Client Care Supervisor, schedulers, the Administrator and any other employees of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect the safety of aides in clients' homes and in the workplace by providing workers' compensation coverage, safe lifting and transfer training, a right to leave an unsafe home, and prompt reporting of injuries and violence.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains and abides by a valid workers' compensation policy covering its affiliated aides (HSC §1796.42(b)). Aides are trained on basic safety precautions and emergency procedures before they work with clients (HSC §1796.44). Aides use safe lifting and transfer techniques, and [AGENCY NAME] does not ask them to lift or transfer in ways they have not been trained for. An aide may leave an unsafe home and call the supervisor without penalty. Aides report all work injuries the same day. As an operator standard, [AGENCY NAME] recognizes that California employers may also owe a written injury and illness prevention program and workplace violence prevention measures. The Administrator will confirm the specific requirements with counsel and adopt a written program that fits [AGENCY NAME]. Where the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030) applies, SAF-03 and the exposure procedures apply.

definitions.definition: A situation in which the aide reasonably believes there is a risk of physical harm, such as threats or violence, weapons displayed, intoxicated or aggressive persons, sexual harassment, fire or structural hazards, or hazardous conditions such as gas odor, severe infestation or unrestrained dangerous animals.
Any act or threat of physical violence, harassment, intimidation or other threatening behavior directed at an employee, whether by a client, family member, visitor, co-worker or stranger.
Methods taught in training for moving or assisting clients, including body mechanics, use of gait belts and approved equipment, and asking for help when a client cannot be moved safely by one person.

procedures: The Administrator keeps the workers' compensation policy in force at all times for all affiliated aides and keeps proof of coverage on file. The Administrator reports any lapse or change in coverage immediately under GOV-03 and REC-02.

Before client contact, each aide is trained on basic safety precautions, emergency procedures and infection control in the 3-hour safety portion of entry-level training (TRN-02, HSC §1796.44). The training includes safe lifting, transfers and body mechanics, and is refreshed annually (TRN-03).

At the home assessment, the Client Care Supervisor checks the home for hazards: clutter, poor lighting, trip hazards, unsafe equipment, smoke or gas hazards, animals, weapons, and the neighborhood. The supervisor also notes any history of aggression by the client or others in the home. Findings are recorded in the service plan (SVC-01, SVC-02).

If a client needs lifting or transfer help that one aide cannot safely give, the supervisor arranges equipment, a second aide, a family member's help or a referral to the client's clinician. If the client's needs are beyond what the aide may do, scope limits in PRG-03 apply. The aide never performs a transfer for which he or she has not been trained.

An aide who feels unsafe at any time may leave the home, taking his or her belongings and the client's safety into account. If the client is helpless and in danger, the aide first calls 911. The aide then calls the Client Care Supervisor or on-call line at [PHONE] and describes what happened.

An aide who leaves an unsafe home in good faith is not disciplined and does not lose pay for the scheduled time. The supervisor assesses the situation, decides on safe arrangements (for example, paired visits, changed hours, family agreements) and arranges backup care so the client is not abandoned (SVC-05). If the problem cannot be resolved, services may be discontinued under SVC-08.

Threats, violence or harassment by anyone are reported by the aide to the supervisor immediately, and by written report the same day. If the aide is in immediate danger, the aide calls 911. The supervisor completes an incident form (SAF-02), and the Administrator follows up with law enforcement, APS or the client's clinician as appropriate.

Aides report every work-related injury or illness to the supervisor the same day, however minor. The supervisor makes sure the aide gets medical care at once if needed, completes the incident form, and starts the workers' compensation claim. [AGENCY NAME] gives the aide the required claim forms within the time required by law and does not discourage or penalize any claim.
If the aide's injury involves blood or body fluids, SAF-03 exposure steps are followed at the same time.
In the office, the Administrator makes sure that entrances, lighting, emergency exits and contact numbers are safe and that staff know what to do in a threatening situation, a fire or an earthquake.
Aides driving for work follow PRG-04 and PER-07. They do not use a phone while driving and report any vehicle accident immediately.

The Administrator will confirm with counsel what California requires for an injury and illness prevention program and workplace violence prevention, adopt a written program, and train staff. This is done within [30] days of the adoption of this manual and the results are filed with the policy manual.
The Administrator reviews injury and violence reports at least quarterly under GOV-05 to find hazards, training needs and unsafe client situations, and records the corrective action.
No employee is retaliated against for reporting an injury, a hazard, a threat or violence, or for leaving an unsafe home. Retaliation is grounds for discipline under PER-09.

responsibilities.duty: Keeps workers' compensation in force, adopts the written safety program after counsel review, and reviews injuries quarterly.
Assesses home safety, arranges equipment or help for transfers, responds to unsafe-home calls and starts injury claims.
Provides backup coverage when an aide leaves an unsafe home and logs on-call contacts.
Uses safe techniques, does not perform untrained transfers, leaves unsafe homes and calls the supervisor, and reports injuries the same day.

documentation: Workers' compensation certificate of coverage (GOV-03)
Entry-level and annual safety training records (TRN-02, TRN-03, TRN-05)
Home safety assessment in the client record (SVC-01)
Incident forms for injuries, threats and unsafe-home departures (SAF-02)
Workers' compensation claim records
Written injury and illness prevention program, when adopted
Quarterly review notes (GOV-05)

policies.title: Client Records and Retention
policies.applies_to: The Administrator and designee, the Client Care Supervisor, schedulers and billing staff, affiliated home care aides, and anyone who creates, uses, stores or destroys client records at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To set what goes in each client record, who may see it, how it is kept secure and available for inspection, and how long it is retained before secure destruction.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps a complete, accurate and confidential record for every client. The Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act (HSC §1796.10 et seq.) sets no records-retention period, so [AGENCY NAME] adopts one as an operator standard. CDSS may inspect books, records and premises through random, unannounced inspections, and refusing access is cause for license revocation (HSC §1796.52). Records are therefore kept organized and accessible at [ADDRESS] or through secure electronic access that an authorized person can open during an inspection. A copy of each suspected-abuse report is kept and available to CDSS during normal business hours (HSC §1796.42(e)). Client records are stored securely with limited access and are retained and destroyed according to the schedule in this policy. To the extent [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, it also meets the administrative requirements of 45 CFR 164.530, including safeguards, workforce training, sanctions and documentation. CR-03 governs privacy and release of information.

definitions.definition: All paper and electronic information about a client: agreement, assessment, service plan, visit notes and timekeeping, incident reports, complaints, correspondence and discharge information.
The separate confidential file holding a copy of each suspected-abuse report made by [AGENCY NAME] or its aides (HSC §1796.42(e)).
The minimum time a record is kept after the client's last date of service before it may be destroyed.
A direction by the Administrator or counsel that records related to a complaint, claim, investigation or lawsuit must not be destroyed.

procedures: The Client Care Supervisor opens a record for each client at intake (SVC-01). The record contains: the signed service agreement with rates and billing disclosure (CR-06); the intake and assessment (SVC-01); the service plan and each update (SVC-02); the client rights notice and acknowledgment (CR-01); privacy notice and releases (CR-03); the emergency plan and medication list (SAF-04); visit notes and timekeeping records (SVC-06); supervisory visit notes (SVC-03); incident reports (SAF-02); complaints and their resolution (CR-02); and discharge or transfer documents (SVC-08).

Aides enter visit notes the same day, in ink or in the approved electronic system. The notes record the tasks performed, the client's condition, and any problem or change. Aides sign or authenticate every entry with the date and time. Late entries are labeled as late and dated when made.

Entries are never erased or backdated. Corrections are made by a single line through the error with the date and initials of the person correcting, or by an audit-tracked correction in the electronic system.

The Administrator keeps the abuse-report file separately from routine client records. It holds a copy of each suspected-abuse report made under WIC §15630 or the Penal Code child abuse reporting provisions. The file is organized so that it can be produced for CDSS on request during normal business hours (HSC §1796.42(e)).

Paper records are kept in locked cabinets in a locked room at [ADDRESS]. Electronic records are kept on a system with unique user names, passwords, role-based access, automatic log-off, encryption, audit logs and regular backups. Only staff with a need to know for their duties may see a client's record.

Staff do not leave client records in vehicles, in homes (beyond what the plan requires), in public places or on personal devices. Records that must be carried are kept in a locked or secure container, and staff report any loss or theft to the Administrator the same day.

Release of client information follows CR-03. Records are released only with the client's written authorization or as permitted or required by law. Requests by clients to review or copy their own records are logged and answered promptly under CR-03.

On a CDSS inspection or complaint investigation, the Administrator or designee gives inspectors prompt access to the books, records and premises requested (HSC §1796.52; see GOV-07). A staff member who is unsure about a request calls the Administrator at [PHONE]. Access is never refused. The Administrator logs what was provided.

Retention schedule (operator standard). Client records, including visit notes, service agreements, plans, incident reports and complaints, are kept for at least seven (7) years after the client's last date of service. Records of a client who was a minor at the time of service are kept until the client is at least 25 years old or for seven years after the last service, whichever is later. Copies of abuse reports are kept at least as long as the related client record. The Administrator may extend a period based on advice from counsel or insurers.
Billing and timekeeping records are kept for at least seven (7) years from the date of service or longer if a payer's contract requires it (SVC-06, SVC-09, GOV-06).

Each January, the Administrator identifies records that have passed their retention period. The Administrator confirms that no legal hold, open complaint, audit, claim or investigation applies and then approves destruction in writing.

Paper records are destroyed by cross-cut shredding or a certified shredding vendor. Electronic records are permanently deleted from all systems and backups, with vendor certification where a vendor is used. A destruction log records the client's record number (not the name), date range, method, date and the person who approved and carried out the destruction.

If [AGENCY NAME] closes or changes ownership, the Administrator arranges for continued secure storage of records for the full retention period and tells CDSS of the arrangements as required by GOV-02. Clients are told where to request their records.

Staff are trained on this policy at hire and annually, and a signed confidentiality statement is kept in the personnel file (PER-06). Misuse of a record or unauthorized access is grounds for discipline under PER-09.
The Administrator checks a sample of client records at least quarterly for completeness, timeliness and security. The Administrator reports the findings under GOV-05 and assigns corrective action.

responsibilities.duty: Controls record systems, keeps the abuse-report file, gives CDSS access, approves destruction and audits records.
Opens and maintains each client record, checks completeness and timeliness of entries.
Maintains timekeeping and billing records and applies the retention schedule to them.
Completes accurate, timely visit notes and protects client information.

documentation: Client record contents list (agreement, assessment, service plan, visit notes, incident reports, complaints)
Abuse-report file with copies of each report (HSC §1796.42(e))
Access list and audit logs for electronic records
Release-of-information and client access request log
Records destruction log with approvals
Legal hold notices
Quarterly record audit results (GOV-05)
Signed staff confidentiality statements (PER-06)

policies.title: Required Reports and Notifications to the State
policies.applies_to: Licensee, Administrator, designee, Client Care Supervisor, Scheduler/Registry and Billing Coordinator, and all affiliated home care aides
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] gives the California Department of Social Services (CDSS), Community Care Licensing Division, Home Care Services Branch (HCSB), and the responsible protective agencies every report, notice, list, fee and renewal filing the Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act requires. Reports must be complete, timely and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will make every required report and notification to the State of California on time, in writing where required, and will keep proof of each one. (1) Aide separation: the agency will immediately notify CDSS when it no longer employs an individual as an affiliated home care aide (HSC §1796.43(a)(3), citation C12). (2) Abuse reporting: the agency will report suspected or known abuse of a dependent adult or elder as required by Welfare and Institutions Code §15630, and suspected or known child abuse as required by Penal Code §§11164-11174.3. It will keep a copy of EACH suspected-abuse report and make it available to CDSS for review during normal business hours (HSC §1796.42(e), citation C10). (3) Aide list and proof of compliance: on CDSS request, the agency will provide a complete list of its affiliated aides and proof that each meets the aide requirements of HSC §§1796.43, 1796.44 and 1796.45 (HSC §1796.37(a)(5), citation C4). (4) Licensure maintenance: the agency will renew its license every 2 years with the fee postmarked on or before the expiration date, keep required insurance, workers' compensation and bond proof current, cooperate with CDSS, and carry no outstanding fees or civil penalties (HSC §1796.37(a)(2)-(4), (a)(8), (a)(13) and (b), citation C4). (5) Changes: the agency will notify CDSS of a change of location (current fee $100) or a change in corporation (current fee $200) and pay the fee set under HSC §1796.49 (citation C16). The agency does not wait for a CDSS reminder. CDSS mails a renewal fee notice at least 60 days before the renewal date (HSC §1796.37(c)), but timely renewal is the licensee's responsibility whether or not the notice arrives. No employee may delay, alter, withhold or discourage a required report. Retaliation against anyone who makes a report in good faith is prohibited.

procedures: Required Reports Calendar: The Administrator maintains a Required Reports Calendar in the compliance file. It lists the license expiration date, the renewal-fee mailing target, insurance and bond expiration dates, and a standing entry for aide separation notices. The Administrator reviews it on the first business day of each month and records the review.

Aide separation, same-day notice: When any aide separates, the Client Care Supervisor notifies the Administrator on the day the separation is known or decided. The Administrator or designee notifies CDSS that the person is no longer employed by [AGENCY NAME] the same business day, which meets the 'immediately' standard. The notice goes by the method CDSS directs for registry or HCSB communications (Guardian/Home Care Aide Registry, or HCSB at HCSB@dss.ca.gov or (877) 424-5778). See PER-10.

Aide separation, record: The person making the notice saves the confirmation (screenshot, email or call log with date, time, CDSS staff name) in the aide's personnel file (PER-06) and enters it on the Separation Notice Log. The Scheduler/Registry and Billing Coordinator removes the aide from active scheduling and the active aide roster on the same day.

Suspected abuse, immediate action: Any employee who observes or suspects abuse of an elder, dependent adult or child must follow PER-02 and PRG-05 and make the required mandated report directly. The employee may not wait for a supervisor's approval, and informs the Client Care Supervisor and Administrator after the report has been made or at the same time. Make the report by telephone immediately or as soon as practicably possible. If there is immediate danger, call 911 first.

Suspected abuse, written follow-up: Where the law requires a written report after the telephone report, the reporter completes it within the statutory deadline. Agency standard: the same day as the telephone report. The Administrator or designee confirms it was sent and checks that the report names the agency, client, aide (if relevant), date, and facts observed.

Abuse report copies: The reporter, or the Administrator if the reporter cannot, places a copy of EACH suspected-abuse report in the Abuse Report File, together with proof of the telephone report (date, time, agency, name of person spoken to) and proof of transmittal of the written report. These copies are kept as a separate file from the client record so they can be produced quickly, and are retained under the REC-01 retention schedule.

Abuse report availability to CDSS: The Administrator or designee will produce the Abuse Report File to any CDSS representative who asks to review it during normal business hours. Copies are never destroyed, altered or removed from the file without Administrator approval documented under REC-01. The agency does not disclose more of the client's information to others than the law allows (CR-03).

Incident link: When a reportable event is also an incident (SAF-02), the Administrator cross-references the Incident Report and the abuse report copy and confirms the abuse report was made before closing the incident.

Aide list and proof of compliance: The Scheduler/Registry and Billing Coordinator keeps a current Affiliated Aide Roster showing for each aide: name, registry/registration status and expiration, Live Scan/background clearance date, TB clearance date, entry-level training completion date, and annual training hours. This roster supports the requirements of HSC §§1796.43, 1796.44 and 1796.45 (PER-03, PER-04, PER-05, TRN-05).

Responding to a CDSS request: On receiving a CDSS request for the aide list, the Administrator logs the date and time and the requester's name. The Scheduler produces the roster and the supporting proof for each aide and the Administrator reviews it for completeness. The package goes to CDSS by the deadline CDSS gives, or within [NUMBER OF DAYS] business days if none is given, and a copy of what was sent is kept in the compliance file.

Gaps found: If the review finds an aide who lacks required proof, the Administrator removes that aide from client assignments until the gap is cured (PER-01, TRN-01) and informs CDSS accurately about the gap in the response. No document is created after the fact or backdated.

License renewal, advance work: The license renews every 2 years. The Administrator starts renewal at least 120 days before the license expiration date. The agency does not rely on the CDSS fee notice, which CDSS mails at least 60 days before the renewal date. If no notice has arrived 60 days before expiration, the Administrator contacts HCSB at (877) 424-5778.

License renewal, requirements check: Before renewal the Administrator confirms the items required for licensure are current: $1M/$3M liability insurance, workers' compensation (policy number, dates, carrier name and address), the $10,000 employee dishonesty bond with third-party coverage, no outstanding fees or civil penalties, and any other CDSS renewal items (GOV-02, GOV-03). Any changes to prior licensed-facility roles or discipline disclosures are reported as CDSS requires.

License renewal, payment: The Administrator prepares the renewal fee in the amount on the CDSS notice (the current schedule is $5,603 per 2 years) and sends it by trackable mail so that it is postmarked on or before the expiration date. Agency standard: postmark at least 10 calendar days before expiration. The postmark or delivery confirmation and a copy of the payment are kept in the compliance file.

Change of location: Before moving the office, the Administrator contacts HCSB, submits the change of location notice and the $100 fee by the method CDSS directs, and confirms in writing what CDSS requires before operations begin at the new address. The new license is posted when issued (PRG-02), and the new address is updated in client agreements, brochures, advertising and the website (GOV-02).

Change in corporation: Before any change in the licensed legal entity, ownership structure or governing body that may be a change in corporation, the licensee consults HCSB, submits the change notice and the $200 fee, and does not operate under the new structure until CDSS confirms what is required. The Administrator updates the board/governing body records (GOV-01).

Fees and penalties: The Administrator pays any CDSS fee or civil penalty by its due date and records it in the compliance file. No renewal or change request is submitted while a fee or civil penalty is outstanding (HSC §1796.37(a)(8)).

Cooperation with CDSS: All employees direct CDSS inspectors and investigators to the Administrator or designee. The Administrator or designee provides prompt, honest cooperation, access to requested records and answers to questions during normal business hours (GOV-07).

Quarterly audit: Each quarter the Administrator audits the Separation Notice Log against payroll and termination records to confirm every separated aide was reported to CDSS, compares the Abuse Report File to the Incident Log, and reports the results and any corrective action at the next Quality Assurance meeting (GOV-05).

Personnel Policies – Abuse Reporting Procedures: At a minimum, documentation must indicate that employees will be informed of their responsibilities to report to appropriate agencies per Health and Safety Code Section 1796.42.

Personnel Policies – Hiring Practices: Documentation must include informing employees that conditions of their employment include fingerprint clearance, statement of prior criminal convictions, TB clearance, and registration on the Home Care Aide Registry.

Training Plan for Affiliated Home Care Aides, submitted to CDSS at the time of application. For both entry-level and annual training, the plan must include proposals on who will be conducting the training, written description of the objectives, and the title and duration of the training as specified in Health and Safety Code Section 1796.44.

Entry-Level Training: An Affiliated Home Care Aide must complete a minimum of five (5) hours of entry-level training prior to presence with a client. Training must include: Two (2) hours of orientation training regarding his/her role as a caregiver and terms of employment; and Three (3) hours of basic health and safety training, including but not limited to: Infection Control; Emergency Procedures

Annual Training: A minimum of five (5) hours of annual training that relates to core competencies and is population specific. Proposed training must include but not be limited to these topics: Clients rights and safety; How to provide for and respond to a client's daily living needs; How to report, prevent, and detect abuse and neglect; How to assist a client with personal hygiene and other home care services; and How to safely transport a client (if applicable).

Sample training verification log must be included with the training plan. At a minimum, the log must include: employees name; hire date; position title; registration date; training title and brief description of topics covered; month/day/year training was completed; training hours received; Instructor/trainer first and last name (if in-person training); organization delivering the training; and location of training (if online, please specify website).

official.notes: HCS 281 is an application booklet. No separate policy checklist form or regulation lists the required written policies for HCOs. The booklet itself says regulations are still being developed, with Written Directives to follow. Applicants mail one complete packet to CDSS Home Care Services Branch, 744 P Street, Sacramento, CA 95814 with the fee. The Section A forms and Section B supplemental documents must go in the same sequence as the booklet lists them. CDSS returns the whole packet if it is incomplete. The booklet requires original signatures and dates, and tells applicants to keep a photocopy. The Section B order is B1 (organizational documents), B2 Job Descriptions, B3 Personnel Policies, B4 Training Plan, B5 Program Description, B6 (insurance). So organize the manual as separately tabbed B2–B5 documents, with B1 and B6 handled as other application paperwork. The booklet gives no item numbers inside B2–B5. The IDs above (B2(a), B3(a), B4(a) and so on) are my labels for the bullets in the document's own order. B3 says Personnel Policies 'should include' the abuse-reporting and hiring items. The booklet notes that CDSS does not enforce other agencies' rules, such as minimum wage and Fair Employment Practices, but applicants should check for conflicts. B5 allows the program description to be a pamphlet, brochure or other document as long as all four elements are included. The booklet says nothing on discipline, medication, disaster plans, complaint procedures or similar topics, so I did not add any. The 8/15 B4 text may predate current training rules (HSC §1796.44 as amended by SB 412), so check the current HCS 281 and the statute.
